answer.label: Not Hippocrates — an unsourced modern saying
answer.authorDates: No documented author, work or date · not in the Hippocratic Corpus
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears in no Hippocratic treatise, and the quote lists that carry it never name one. Helen King, who wrote the standard study of how Hippocrates is used online, examined this exact saying and ruled it out as Hippocratic. The nearest genuine passage — section XIX of the treatise On Nutriment — says something quite different, and it is the seed of a different saying altogether.

source.excerpt: Leave your drugs in the chemist’s pot if you can heal the patient with food.
trail: Classicist Helen King examines this exact saying in Hippocrates Now: The ‘Father of Medicine’ in the Internet Age (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020) ↗ and rules it out as Hippocratic, noting that the quote lists carrying it never attach a treatise to it.

Wikiquote’s Hippocrates page ↗ does not carry the line at all. Its Disputed section handles the better-known cousin, “Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food”, recording that it does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus.
The quote sites that spread it supply no citation whatsoever: AZQuotes ↗ prints the line under Hippocrates’ name with no work, no date and no edition attached.

The nearest real text is section XIX of the Hippocratic treatise On Nutriment, preserved in Greek at Greek Wikisource ↗ — a compressed aphorism about medication in food, with nothing about chemists, pots or setting drugs aside.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to give, because there is no original. The closest real passage is section XIX of the Hippocratic treatise On Nutriment: «ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη ἄριστον, ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη φλαῦρον, φλαῦρον καὶ ἄριστον πρός τι» — roughly, that medication taken in food may be excellent or may be bad, bad or good according to circumstances. W. H. S. Jones read the key word narrowly, as purging rather than medicine in general. Either way it is the seed of the famous “Let food be thy medicine”, not of this line, and it mentions no chemist and no pot.

source.rightsNote: No work, author or first publication can be tied to this English wording, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The ancient Greek of On Nutriment is long out of copyright, but that is a different sentence in a different language; the line circulating under Hippocrates’ name has no identified translator, edition or date behind it.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.heading: About Hippocrates
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician, called the Father of Medicine
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos was a Greek physician of the classical period, later canonised as the Father of Medicine. Almost nothing survives that can be proved to be his own writing: the treatises of the Hippocratic Corpus are anonymous, span several centuries, and are reckoned by scholars to involve around nineteen different hands. Diet genuinely was central to that tradition — but its texts treat food and drugs as different kinds of intervention, which is close to the opposite of what this saying asks a doctor to do.

misattribution.heading: How it travels
misattribution.intro: This is a wellness-poster line, not a medical text. It moves with Hippocrates’ name attached and nothing else — no treatise, no page, no translator — and it usually appears alongside the more famous “Let food be thy medicine”.

items.why: Helen King examined this exact sentence in Hippocrates Now ↗ and concluded it is not Hippocratic; she also flags ‘chemist’s pot’ as an odd phrase in its own right. A pharmacist’s dispensing pot is a modern British image, not a fifth-century BC Greek one — that anachronism is our own observation, not King’s.

“Leave thy drugs in the chemist’s pot if thou canst heal the patient with food.” King found this thee-and-thou dressing-up in Gunther B. Paulien’s The Divine Prescription and Science of Health and Healing (Fort Oglethorpe, GA: TEACH Services, 1995), which uses the saying twice — once plainly, once archaised. See her discussion ↗.

“Heal” and “cure” are used interchangeably across the quote sites, and King records both forms in circulation — what usually happens to a line with no fixed text behind it. Details in Hippocrates Now ↗.

One health-site quote list gave the line the date 420 BCE, and attached treatise names to some of its other Hippocrates quotations — but not to this one. King records the page and notes that the account was later suspended; see her endnotes ↗.

“Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food” is the line this one rides alongside. Wikiquote files it under Disputed ↗, following Diana Cardenas’s 2013 paper showing it is a misquotation rather than a Hippocratic sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: No Hippocratic text tells a doctor to leave the drugs in the pot. Helen King’s Hippocrates Now ↗ takes the saying apart and concludes flatly that “it is not Hippocratic” — and nobody, in all the years it has been in print, has produced the source.

context.heading: Why this one spreads
lead: Hippocrates is one of the internet’s most reliable rubber stamps. Attach his name to a claim about diet and it arrives pre-approved by twenty-four centuries of medicine, which is exactly why supplement sellers, detox programmes and organic-produce sites reach for him. Helen King’s book exists because the pattern became pervasive enough that the invented Hippocrates now shapes what people believe about the real one.

The irony is that the sentiment is not merely unsourced but faintly un-Hippocratic. Hippocratic therapy took diet extremely seriously — regimen was the physician’s first instrument — but the texts, and Galen after them, keep food and drugs in separate categories: food sustains the body as it is, medicine pushes it to behave differently. A slogan that asks you to pick one over the other flattens a distinction the tradition was careful about.
context.detailsSummary: What the Hippocratic texts actually say about food
detailsBody: The passage everyone is reaching for is section XIX of On Nutriment, a short, gnomic treatise whose dating is itself contested. W. H. S. Jones placed it around 400 BC on stylistic grounds; more recent scholarship puts it in the second or first century BC, with Heinrich von Staden describing it as self-consciously archaising — an unsuccessful attempt at Hippocratic authenticity. On that later dating it postdates the historical Hippocrates by centuries.

Diana Cardenas’s 2013 paper in the e-SPEN Journal traced how the food-as-medicine aphorism spread through the medical literature and showed it to be a literary creation rather than a quotation. Her argument is not that diet was unimportant to Hippocratic medicine, but close to the reverse of the popular reading: collapsing food into medicine misrepresents how the ancient texts actually worked.
context.pull: A saying with no source is not ancient wisdom. It is a modern slogan wearing a toga.

sourcesVerified.claim: OAPEN hosts the open-access full text of Helen King, Hippocrates Now: The 'Father of Medicine' in the Internet Age (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020, ISBN 9781350005891). That text states of 'Leave your drugs in the chemist's pot if you can heal the patient with food' that 'it is not Hippocratic'; it also records the 'cure' variant, the archaised 'Leave thy drugs in the chemist's pot if thou canst heal the patient with food' in Gunther B. Paulien's The Divine Prescription and Science of Health and Healing (Fort Oglethorpe, GA: TEACH Services, 1995), a quote list dating the line to 420 BCE whose account was later suspended, King's remark that 'chemist's pot' is an odd phrase, and the discussion of On Nutriment 19 including Jones's dating and von Staden's 'self-consciously archaizing' characterisation.

Wikiquote's Hippocrates page does not contain the phrase 'chemist's pot' anywhere; its Disputed section carries 'Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food' with the note that it does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus, citing Diana Cardenas, and quotes On Nutriment 19 in Greek.
Greek Wikisource's text of Περί τροφής (On Nutriment) contains at section XIX the line «Ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη ἄριστον, ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη φλαῦρον, φλαῦρον καὶ ἄριστον πρός τι.»

The DOI resolves to Diana Cardenas, 'Let not thy food be confused with thy medicine: The Hippocratic misquotation', e-SPEN Journal, vol. 8, no. 6, pp. e260-e262, 2013. Verified against the Crossref record for this DOI (api.crossref.org), which returns exactly that title, journal, volume, issue, pagination, author and year, and confirmed the DOI redirects to the Elsevier article page for PII S2212826313000924.

Wikipedia's Hippocratic Corpus article states that none of the texts are proven to have been written by Hippocrates himself, that the corpus is a collection of anonymous authors spanning centuries with at least nineteen different hands identified, and lists 'On Aliment or Nutriment' among the works.
Wikipedia's Hippocrates article gives his dates as c. 460 - c. 370 BC and describes him as a Greek physician and philosopher of the classical period, traditionally called the Father of Medicine.
AZQuotes carries 'Leave your drugs in the chemist's pot if you can heal the patient with food.' attributed to Hippocrates with no book, publication, citation or date given.

Quote Investigator has no article on this quote: a site search for "chemist's pot" returns 'Nothing Found', and a site search for 'Hippocrates' returns only the 2019 article on 'It Is Quite As Important To Know What Kind of a Patient the Disease Has Got'.
